feedback.problem: At which points on the surface $z={x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}+2y$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨-4,0,1⟩?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2x+2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x+2,\,2y+2,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-4,0,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2x+2,\,2y+2,\,-1⟩=⟨-4,0,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}c(2x+2)=-4 \\ c(2y+2)=0 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-(2x+2)=-4\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-(2y+2)=0\,⟹\,y=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =(1)^{2}+2(1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(1,-1,2).$
